run.script_question: Can the sequence be chosen by a name supplied at run time?
run.prerequisite: R3 PASSED on 2026-11-03 (see R3_01_r3_sequence_in_udf_20261103-204457.json) - a SQL UDF body may contain seq.NEXTVAL.
run.executed_by: Cortex Code (sql_execute, one statement per call)

statements.sql: CREATE OR REPLACE SEQUENCE w6_employee_seq START 1 INCREMENT 1
CREATE OR REPLACE SEQUENCE w6_job_seq START 1000 INCREMENT 1

statements.purpose: Fully-qualified sequence name inside the function body. Hard-codes database + schema, so NOT portable for R8.
statements.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION w6_qualified_test()
RETURNS NUMBER(38,0)
VOLATILE
AS
$$
    LM_POC_DB.POC_SCHEMA.w6_employee_seq.NEXTVAL
$$

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_out, COUNT(DISTINCT k) AS distinct_keys,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT k) = COUNT(*) THEN 'PASS - qualified name works'
            ELSE 'FAIL' END AS verdict
FROM (SELECT w6_qualified_test() AS k FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 5)))

statements.purpose: Unqualified sequence name - resolved in the schema containing the function, therefore the R8-portable form.
statements.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION w6_unqualified_test()
RETURNS NUMBER(38,0)
VOLATILE
AS
$$
    w6_employee_seq.NEXTVAL
$$

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_out, COUNT(DISTINCT k) AS distinct_keys,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT k) = COUNT(*) THEN 'PASS - unqualified name works'
            ELSE 'FAIL' END AS verdict
FROM (SELECT w6_unqualified_test() AS k FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 5)))
statements.expectation: 5 / 5 / PASS. If both pass -> use the UNQUALIFIED form in the real function, for R8.

statements.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE w6_sequence_registry (
    LOGICAL_NAME       VARCHAR(100),
    FULL_SEQUENCE_NAME VARCHAR(500)
)

INSERT INTO w6_sequence_registry VALUES
    ('EMPLOYEE', 'w6_employee_seq'),
    ('JOB',      'w6_job_seq')

statements.purpose: Registry-table indirection: hold the sequence name in a table, read it, use it via IDENTIFIER(). EXPECTED TO FAIL - the error message is the evidence.
statements.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION w6_registry_lookup_test(logical_name VARCHAR)
RETURNS NUMBER(38,0)
VOLATILE
AS
$$
    (SELECT IDENTIFIER(r.FULL_SEQUENCE_NAME || '.NEXTVAL')
     FROM w6_sequence_registry r
     WHERE r.LOGICAL_NAME = logical_name)
$$

error.message:
Compilation of SQL UDF failed: SQL compilation error:
syntax error line 2 at position 5 unexpected 'SELECT'.
syntax error line 2 at position 23 unexpected 'r'.
syntax error line 3 at position 5 unexpected 'FROM'.

statements.expectation: a compilation error, at CREATE or at first call
statements.observation: Failed at CREATE, so the function never existed and no invocation was possible. The documented cause is 'Dynamic SQL is not supported when referring to database objects' plus IDENTIFIER() accepting only a string literal, session variable, bind variable or Snowflake Scripting variable - a column value is none of those.

statements.purpose: IDENTIFIER() straight on the parameter, no table involved. Isolates whether the registry read or the parameter is the blocker.
statements.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION w6_param_identifier_test(seq_name VARCHAR)
RETURNS NUMBER(38,0)
VOLATILE
AS
$$
    IDENTIFIER(seq_name).NEXTVAL
$$

error.message:
Compilation of SQL UDF failed: SQL compilation error:
syntax error line 2 at position 15 unexpected 'seq_name'.
syntax error line 2 at position 15 unexpected 'seq_name'.
syntax error line 2 at position 24 unexpected '.'.

statements.expectation: the same failure, confirming the PARAMETER is the blocker so no amount of table indirection can help
statements.observation: Fails with no table in the picture. The parameter itself cannot feed IDENTIFIER(), which settles the question: table indirection cannot rescue the approach.

statements.purpose: The branch selector - run-time value picks a branch; every sequence is named literally, so no identifier is ever constructed from data.
statements.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION w6_branch_selector(sequence_name VARCHAR)
RETURNS NUMBER(38,0)
VOLATILE
COMMENT = 'VOLATILE is required - see 04_r10_concurrency.sql T4.4/T4.5.'
AS
$$
    CASE sequence_name
        WHEN 'EMPLOYEE_SEQ' THEN w6_employee_seq.NEXTVAL
        WHEN 'JOB_SEQ'      THEN w6_job_seq.NEXTVAL
    END
$$

SELECT requested,
       COUNT(*) AS rows_out,
       COUNT(DISTINCT k) AS distinct_keys,
       MIN(k) AS min_key, MAX(k) AS max_key,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT k) = COUNT(*) THEN 'PASS' ELSE 'FAIL' END AS verdict
FROM (
    SELECT 'EMPLOYEE_SEQ' AS requested, w6_branch_selector('EMPLOYEE_SEQ') AS k
    FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 5))
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'JOB_SEQ', w6_branch_selector('JOB_SEQ')
    FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 5))
)
GROUP BY requested ORDER BY requested
statements.expectation: two rows. EMPLOYEE keys in the 1.. range, JOB keys in the 1000.. range, 5 distinct each, both PASS
statements.observation: Each requested name drew from its own sequence: EMPLOYEE from the 1-origin sequence (201-205 after earlier consumption in T2.1), JOB from the 1000-origin sequence (1005-1009).

statements.sql: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE w6_mixed_stage (LOGICAL_NAME VARCHAR(100))

INSERT INTO w6_mixed_stage VALUES
    ('EMPLOYEE_SEQ'), ('JOB_SEQ'), ('EMPLOYEE_SEQ'), ('JOB_SEQ'), ('EMPLOYEE_SEQ')

statements.purpose: Name varying PER ROW - the realistic case when one function serves several tables in one load.
statements.sql:
WITH keyed AS (
    SELECT LOGICAL_NAME, w6_branch_selector(LOGICAL_NAME) AS k FROM w6_mixed_stage
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_out,
       COUNT(DISTINCT k) AS distinct_keys,
       SUM(CASE WHEN LOGICAL_NAME = 'EMPLOYEE_SEQ' AND k < 1000 THEN 1
                WHEN LOGICAL_NAME = 'JOB_SEQ'      AND k >= 1000 THEN 1
                ELSE 0 END) AS keys_from_correct_sequence,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT k) = COUNT(*)
             AND COUNT(*) = SUM(CASE WHEN LOGICAL_NAME = 'EMPLOYEE_SEQ' AND k < 1000 THEN 1
                                     WHEN LOGICAL_NAME = 'JOB_SEQ'      AND k >= 1000 THEN 1
                                     ELSE 0 END)
            THEN 'PASS - every row keyed from its own sequence'
            ELSE 'FAIL' END AS verdict
FROM keyed
rows: PASS - every row keyed from its own sequence
statements.observation: The branch selector resolves correctly when the sequence name varies row by row, not merely statement by statement.

statements.sql: CREATE OR REPLACE SEQUENCE w6_job_seq START 1000 INCREMENT 1

statements.purpose: Snapshot BEFORE. Measured via INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SEQUENCES.NEXT_VALUE, which reads metadata and consumes nothing - deliberately NOT a bare NEXTVAL, which misled R3's T1.5.
statements.sql:
SELECT SEQUENCE_NAME, NEXT_VALUE, ORDERED
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SEQUENCES
WHERE SEQUENCE_SCHEMA = CURRENT_SCHEMA()
  AND SEQUENCE_NAME IN ('W6_EMPLOYEE_SEQ','W6_JOB_SEQ')
ORDER BY SEQUENCE_NAME
statements.expectation: NEXT_VALUE 1 and 1000. Note ORDERED too - 'NO' means NOORDER.
statements.observation: ORDERED = NO on both sequences. This independently confirms the NOORDER property and is the documented explanation for the non-monotonic values recorded as finding F1 in the R3 run.

statements.purpose: Draw 20 rows, ALL asking for EMPLOYEE_SEQ. JOB_SEQ is never selected.
statements.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_drawn, COUNT(DISTINCT k) AS distinct_keys
FROM (SELECT w6_branch_selector('EMPLOYEE_SEQ') AS k
      FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 20)))

statements.purpose: Snapshot AFTER, and the verdict in one row. THE REAL UNKNOWN: do untaken CASE arms consume sequence values?
statements.sql:
SELECT
    MAX(CASE WHEN SEQUENCE_NAME = 'W6_EMPLOYEE_SEQ' THEN NEXT_VALUE END) AS employee_next,
    MAX(CASE WHEN SEQUENCE_NAME = 'W6_JOB_SEQ'      THEN NEXT_VALUE END) AS job_next,
    CASE WHEN MAX(CASE WHEN SEQUENCE_NAME = 'W6_JOB_SEQ' THEN TO_NUMBER(NEXT_VALUE) END) = 1000
         THEN 'UNTAKEN ARMS ARE FREE - job_seq never moved'
         ELSE 'UNTAKEN ARMS CONSUME - job_seq advanced without being selected'
    END AS verdict
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SEQUENCES
WHERE SEQUENCE_SCHEMA = CURRENT_SCHEMA()
  AND SEQUENCE_NAME IN ('W6_EMPLOYEE_SEQ','W6_JOB_SEQ')
rows: UNTAKEN ARMS CONSUME - job_seq advanced without being selected
statements.expectation: RECORD the number either way. job_next = 1000 -> untaken arms cost nothing. job_next > 1000 -> every arm consumes.
statements.observation: W6_JOB_SEQ advanced from 1000 to 1100 despite never being selected by any row. Both sequences advanced by exactly 100, which is the block-reservation size rather than a per-row cost: 20 rows were drawn, but each referenced sequence reserved a 100-value block.

decision_table_resolution.source: SQL/02_r2_sequence_name_binding.sql - WHAT THE RESULTS MEAN FOR R2
matched_rules: T2.1a+b pass -> use the UNQUALIFIED form in the real function (R8).

T2.2a+b fail -> the registry CANNOT be an indirection inside a UDF. It stays useful as a REGISTRY: generate the function's CASE arms from it, so onboarding a table is still 'insert a row, re-run the generator'.
T2.3a+b pass -> R2 is satisfied by the branch selector. Closes R2.
T2.4 job_seq moved -> add 'one function per sequence' to the build standard, and document the consumption.
decision_table_resolution.answer_to_the_question: The sequence can be chosen by a run-time name ONLY via a branch selector in which every sequence is named literally. A name used to construct an identifier - whether read from a registry table or passed as a parameter - cannot work inside a SQL UDF.
build_standard_decisions: Use the UNQUALIFIED sequence name inside the function body, for R8 portability across environments.
Do NOT attempt registry/IDENTIFIER() indirection inside the UDF. Keep the registry as a code generator for the CASE arms instead.
Prefer one function per sequence as the branch list grows, because of finding F4.

findings.title: Untaken CASE arms DO consume sequence values - every referenced sequence reserves a block
findings.evidence: T2.4a baseline: W6_EMPLOYEE_SEQ NEXT_VALUE = 1, W6_JOB_SEQ NEXT_VALUE = 1000. T2.4b drew 20 rows all requesting EMPLOYEE_SEQ, so the JOB_SEQ arm was never selected. T2.4c after: employee_next = 101, job_next = 1100.
findings.interpretation: W6_JOB_SEQ advanced by 100 without issuing a single key. Both sequences moved by exactly 100 for a 20-row draw, so the cost is block reservation per referenced sequence per statement, not one value per row per arm. This matches the documented wording that each OCCURRENCE of a sequence in the statement generates a set of distinct values - occurrences, not branches taken.
findings.implication: A branch selector with N sequences burns a reserved block from ALL N sequences on every statement, however few arms are actually used. Uniqueness is unaffected. The consequence is wasted consumption and larger gaps, which must be documented so nobody reads the gaps as lost rows. It also argues for one function per sequence once the branch list grows beyond a handful.
findings.status: Open - recommend adding to the build standard.

findings.title: Both sequences are NOORDER, which explains the R3/F1 non-monotonic result
findings.evidence: T2.4a returned ORDERED = NO for both W6_EMPLOYEE_SEQ and W6_JOB_SEQ.
findings.interpretation: NOORDER is the default and is why direct and UDF-mediated calls draw from different reserved ranges, producing values that are unique but not globally ordered.
findings.implication: Confirms finding F1 from the R3 run was expected Snowflake behaviour rather than an anomaly. R10's T4.8 additionally warns against setting ORDER later to tidy the keys, since NOORDER is what makes concurrent INSERTs perform.

findings.title: The T2.2 failures are syntax errors at CREATE, not run-time rejections
findings.evidence: Both T2.2a and T2.2b failed with 'Compilation of SQL UDF failed: SQL compilation error: syntax error ...' at CREATE time. Neither function was ever created, so neither could be invoked.
findings.interpretation: The script allowed for failure 'at CREATE or at first call'. It was at CREATE, and the parser rejects IDENTIFIER() in this position outright rather than deferring to run time.
findings.implication: Useful for the build standard: the failure is loud and immediate, not a silent trap. An engineer attempting the registry approach cannot accidentally ship it.
